citation.title: Real-time multi-objective topology optimization method via deep learning
citation.authors: Cheng Xiang (as printed on the chapter; OpenAlex lists Xiang Cheng), Airong Chen, Dalei Wang, Rujin Ma
citation.venue: In: Bridge Maintenance, Safety, Management, Digitalization and Sustainability (Jensen, Frangopol & Schmidt, eds.), 2024, ISBN 978-1-032-77040-6, pp. 2090-2097 (chapter header and Crossref). Open access via taylorfrancis.com, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0
citation.version_coded: Version of record: publisher chapter PDF (8 pages, pp. 2090-2097) from the Taylor & Francis open-access download link that OpenAlex lists (api.taylorfrancis.com), read in full as text; the results paragraph (p. 2095) and Table 1 and Fig. 4 (p. 2096) also checked on the rendered pages

included.reason: I-QUALITY (screened I-SPEED; the conclusion's only quantitative classical comparison is the share of predictions that beat MMA, a quality result, §5.1 rule 2; the timing appears only in the main text)

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: On the 40x80 cantilever test set, nearly half (49.75%) of the network's predicted designs beat the MMA reference designs, meaning compliance and p-norm stress over 1% lower with volume within 1%.
claim.key_phrase: nearly half of the predicted optimized structures performs better than tradition method
claim.location: Conclusion (Sec. 5, p. 2097), the first quantitative comparison with a classical method there; the share is Table 1 'OR' (p. 2096), defined in Sec. 4 (p. 2095). The abstract compares with the conventional method only qualitatively
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Not applicable to the quality-stratum primary outcome. Alternative (Sec. 4, p. 2095): average MMA time 15.76 s vs 0.0076 s for the network, 15.76 / 0.0076 = 2,074 [derived]; the article states 0.026% of the MMA time and 99.97% saved. These figures disagree: 0.0076 / 15.76 = 0.048% [derived], and the stated parts (9.4 x 10^-4 s preprocessing plus 4.42 x 10^-3 s prediction) sum to 0.0054 s, not 0.0076 s [derived]. Dataset generation and training are excluded, as the article states.
claim.alternatives: (1) Sec. 4 and Table 1 (speed; emphasised by the title and abstract): average 0.0076 s vs 15.76 s for MMA, 99.97% time saved, with mean compliance error -7.50%, p-norm stress error -5.08%, volume error 0.84%, pixel error 5.18% and 5.9% large-error samples. (2) Abstract, qualitative: a large cut in computing cost with little loss of design performance. (3) Conclusion, qualitative: significantly improved computing efficiency.

baseline.classical_method: Compliance minimization with a volume constraint and a p-norm (p = 6) von Mises stress constraint, SIMP interpolation, density filter radius 1.5, solved by MMA (Svanberg 1987) (Sec. 2, Sec. 3.1)
baseline.problem_size: 40 x 80 element cantilever (Sec. 3.1); about 6,640 DOFs [derived: 2 x 41 x 81 = 6,642]; network input 2 x 41 x 81
baseline.classical_iterations: not stated; the text says only that hundreds of FE and sensitivity iterations are needed (Sec. 4)
baseline.ml_time: 0.0076 s average, stated as 9.4 x 10^-4 s preprocessing plus 4.42 x 10^-3 s prediction (Sec. 4, p. 2095); the parts sum to 0.0054 s [derived]
baseline.training_time: not stated; training stopped after 136 epochs (Sec. 3.3); training time is excluded from the reported time (Sec. 4)
baseline.data_generation_cost: 20,000 MMA samples split 8:1:1 (Sec. 3.1); time not stated and excluded from the reported time (Sec. 4) [about 87.6 h at 15.76 s per sample, derived]
baseline.quality_metric: Relative errors of the predicted designs against the MMA designs for compliance (Ec), p-norm stress, volume fraction and pixel accuracy; share of outperforming samples (OR: volume error within 1%, compliance and p-norm stress errors below -1%); large-error rate (LER: compliance or p-norm stress error above 20%) (Sec. 4, Table 1). The FE evaluation of the predicted designs and any thresholding are not described; the compliance and stress values of predicted designs in Fig. 4 imply an FE analysis [inferred]
baseline.quality_gap: Averages (Table 1): Ec -7.50%, p-norm stress error -5.08%, volume error 0.84%, pixel error 5.18%, OR 49.75%, LER 5.90%. Fig. 4(a) examples, network vs MMA: C 105.741 vs 115.910, 101.975 vs 105.860, 121.126 vs 134.774. Fig. 4(b) large-error example: C 166.96 vs 187.95 with p-norm stress 1.342 vs 0.886

R1.evidence: Stratum Q; R1 applies as written (PROTOCOL §11, 2026-09-24). Sec. 4 (p. 2095), Table 1 (p. 2096): predictions and MMA designs are compared on the same test inputs through compliance, p-norm stress and volume errors. Matching is loose: 'outperform' admits a volume difference of up to 1% (mean volume error 0.84%), the MMA stopping rule and iteration count are not stated (only 'hundreds of iterations'), and the MMA references are beaten on average (Ec -7.50%, p-norm stress -5.08%), which suggests under-converged or locally optimal references [inferred]. 5.9% of predictions have errors above 20%.

R2.evidence: Stratum Q (PROTOCOL §11, 2026-09-24): R2 applies only through criterion (b). The abstract (p. 2090) gives no baseline figure and names no weaker baseline; the results compare with the same MMA method (Sec. 3.1, p. 2092; Sec. 4, p. 2095), so (b) is not observed. For the alternative speed outcome: MMA implementation, solver and hardware are not stated; about 6,640 DOFs [derived], so (c) does not apply; (d) and (e) are not established.

R3.evidence: The primary outcome is quality only. For C3 and the alternative speed outcome: Sec. 4 states that dataset generation (20,000 MMA runs, Sec. 3.1) and training (136 epochs, Sec. 3.3) are excluded from the reported time, and neither cost is given; no break-even. [derived] At 15.76 s per MMA run the data alone cost about 87.6 h and are recovered after about 20,000 uses. If the speed outcome is taken as primary, R3 = fail (R3-no-cost).

R4.evidence: Sec. 4, Table 1, Fig. 4: compliance and p-norm stress of the returned predictions are reported against MMA, which implies FE analysis of the predicted designs [inferred; the procedure is not described]. Volume error is reported (mean 0.84%) and large-error samples are counted (5.9%), with disconnected designs named as one cause. The Fig. 4 examples have no stated selection rule but supplement aggregate metrics.

reporting.n_test_cases: about 2,000 test samples [derived: 20,000 x 1/10; Sec. 3.1]; Table 1 gives averages only

notes: Screening code was I-SPEED; the full text gives stratum Q by §5.1 rule 2. Stratum check for the verifier: 'nearly half' in the conclusion is read as a quantitative comparison because it restates Table 1's OR = 49.75%. If it is read as qualitative, the first main-text comparison is Sec. 4 / Table 1, and rule 4 (title 'Real-time'; the abstract stresses computing cost) selects the speed result: stratum speed, claimed speed-up 2,074 [derived], with would-be verdicts R1 partial (quality reported, MMA stopping rule unstated), R2 pass (no marker established), R3 fail (R3-no-cost: data generation and training excluded and not reported) and R4 as coded. This batch applies the same rule-2-then-rule-4 reading to P00161 and P00080. Internal inconsistencies (Sec. 4): the time parts sum to 0.0054 s, not 0.0076 s; the stated 0.026% does not equal 0.0076 / 15.76 = 0.048% [derived]. Duplicate check: P00645 (Thin-Walled Structures 2022, stress-based, closed access) and P01163 (2022 proceedings chapter, stress-based U-Net) are earlier single-objective studies by the same group; P00919 (Scientific Reports 2025, two-stage SwinUnet MOTO with physics-informed refinement and 1,650 samples per condition) extends this method. All three are different studies [inferred from titles, abstracts and this chapter's reference list], so FT-DUPLICATE does not apply. Type: an 8-page paper in an edited proceedings volume, admitted as a conference paper under §3.3 [inferred from format]. The chapter has no hardware, software, code or data statements. Authors checked: no author named Jun Wang. Adjudicator check (2026-09-24): the chapter PDF was re-read in full from the publisher's open-access link (api.taylorfrancis.com, served from the publisher's content store; a first request from another HTTP client met a Cloudflare page and was not pursued). The adjudicator keeps stratum Q: the conclusion (p. 2097) holds one quantitative classical comparison, the nearly-half share, while its efficiency claim has no number, and §5.1 rule 4 is applied only among candidates at the same level (as in P00080 and P00161 of this batch).

stratum.reason: The abstract (p. 2090) states the cost reduction only qualitatively. The conclusion (Sec. 5, p. 2097) holds one quantitative classical comparison, that nearly half of the predictions beat the traditional method (Table 1 OR 49.75%, p. 2096), while its efficiency claim has no number, so §5.1 rule 2 takes it over the main-text timing of Sec. 4 (p. 2095), as the abstract's quality comparison was taken over a main-text 40,000x in P01813. Rule 4 chooses among candidates at one level and does not reach the main text here.

R1.reason: R1 applies as written in stratum Q (§11). Predictions and MMA designs share the test inputs, but the MMA stopping rule and iteration count are not stated (Sec. 4, p. 2095: only 'hundreds of iterations'), and the predictions' volume deviates by 0.84% on average while the 'outperform' share tolerates up to 1% (p. 2095; Table 1, p. 2096): the §5.3 R1 partial case. The second coder's pass judged the speed claim, which is the alternative outcome here.

R2.reason: With stratum Q decided, R2 applies only through criterion (b) (§11). The abstract (p. 2090) gives no baseline figure, and the results use the same MMA method (Sec. 3.1, p. 2092; Sec. 4, p. 2095), so (b) is not observed; the second coder's partial (hardware not stated) concerns the speed alternative.

R3.reason: R3 is na in stratum Q (§11). For the speed alternative the verdict would be fail, not pass: Sec. 4 (p. 2095) says data generation and training are excluded but reports neither cost, and the §5.3 R3 pass case needs both costs reported.

claimed_speedup.reason: The quality-stratum primary outcome carries no speed factor, as decided for P00051 and P01813. The derived 15.76 / 0.0076 = 2,074 (Sec. 4, p. 2095) stays in claimed_speedup_basis as the speed alternative, with the article's inconsistent 0.026% and 99.97% figures.
